newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwanda's first trial on 1994 genocide opens.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda's first trial on 1994 genocide opens.

text.p: Rwanda's first genocide trial opened on Friday with the accused facing the death penalty if convicted on charges of taking part in the slaughter in 1994 of some 800,000 Tutsis along with moderate Hutus.

Rwandan state radio broadcast live the opening of the trial of Deo Bizimana, a former medical assistant, and Egide Gatanazi, a former local administrator, both accused of organising massacres during the killing of about 75 percent of the country's Tutsis.

They are the first suspects to be tried under a genocide law. There are about 90,000 Rwandans crammed into jails since being accused of taking part in the 1994 slaughter by Hutu troops, militiamena and mobs.
Both men at Kibungo, 100 km (60 miles) southeast of Kigali, are accused under category one of the law, said Marie Van der Elst, spokeswoman for the U.N. Human Commissioner for Human Rights.
They are both accused of organising massacres and if convicted by the tribunal are liable to the death penalty.
Tribunals consist of three judges each and trials are expected to last several days. There is one chance of appeal.
Justice ministry officials say they hope that within the next month 12 tribunals will be operating across the country.
They say they do not plan trials for all detained suspects because they believe many will confess in return for leniency.

A Hutu refugee lobby group, the Rally for the Return of Refugees and Democracy to Rwanda (RDR), dismissed the trials as "a mockery of justice" by the Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF), which took power in July 1994 and ended the killings.
The RDR said more than 2,000 Rwandan refugees detained since returning from Zaire in November and Tanzania this month were falsely accused of genocide by people who wanted their property.
"The RPF is opening the second trials of 'genocide suspects', a trial that is going to be nothing but a political trial, a mockery of justice," the RDR said in a statment.
The Rwandan government argues the trials are the only way to end a cycle of impunity and to show that justice is being done.
An international tribunal on the Rwandan genocide opened its first trials at its headquarters in Arusha, Tanzania, this year but it cannot impose the death penalty on those found guilty.
Last year on the first anniversary of the genocide, Rwandan authorities began trials of a number of suspects but they were abandoned in part because there was no law covering genocide.
A second trial of two suspects before a tribunal is expected to start in the capital Kigali on Monday. Both could also face the death peanlty if convicted, Van der Elst said by telephone.
The genocide law, passed in August, divides accused into four categories.
The first is "planners, organisers, instigators, supervisors and leaders" of genocide of a crime against humanity including notorious murderers and persons who committed acts of sexual torture.
The second covers those who participated in the genocide or committed homicide. The third includes those guilty of serious assault. Category four deals with offences against property.
Those who confess or plead guilty can have their sentences reduced.
